source.title: Advancing Deep Residual Learning by Solving the Crux of Degradation in Spiking Neural Networks
source.authors: Yifan Hu; Yujie Wu; Lei Deng; Guoqi Li

record.tranche_reason: Tests depth-related degradation and residual block designs in directly trained spiking neural networks, a new setting for the mapped shortcut claim.
record.gate_note: Reports CIFAR-10 accuracy across depth and residual block designs, plus a textual result for removing interblock LIF functions. These results test V3 in SNNs. The paper does not report the zero-training-error behavior in V1 or the other mapped claim versions.
record.test_reason: The study uses residual learning to develop directly trained spiking neural networks. V3 concerns conventional artificial neural networks; the SNN results measure a related phenomenon in a different kind of system. The reported accuracies also do not establish the training-error comparisons V3 names. No other version is tested.
record.authors_conclusion: The paraphrase is substantially accurate: the authors identify interblock LIF-related information loss as the crux of degradation in directly trained SNNs and propose redesigned residual blocks enabling 482-layer CIFAR-10 and 104-layer ImageNet models without reported degradation. This is their interpretation of the SNN experiments, not a demonstrated failure of residual shortcuts in conventional ANNs.
record.recipe_differences: Direct surrogate-gradient/BPTT training of spiking neural networks; evaluates CIFAR-10 depth and residual block designs rather than the original ANN training recipes.
record.method_sensitivity: Outcome changes with residual block design: retaining interblock LIF with adjusted shortcut signals only alleviates degradation, while the removing structures avoid it through tested depths.

fits_no_version.finding: Canonical spiking residual networks degrade with depth despite BN and shortcuts; the introduction explicitly describes declining training and testing accuracy. Table 2 reports PlainResNet accuracy falling from 85.40% at depth 32 to 72.36% at depth 56.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Transplanting canonical residual blocks into directly trained LIF-based SNNs does not necessarily prevent depth-related degradation.

fits_no_version.finding: Retaining interblock LIF with adjusted shortcut signals only alleviates degradation. Removing or relocating interblock LIF permits deeper SNNs: the three removing designs improve reported accuracy through depth 110, and SRM-ResNet482 reaches 91.9%.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In the tested directly trained SNNs, interblock LIF placement and an uninterrupted identity path determine whether residual architectures avoid degradation with depth.

record.problems: The depth analysis intentionally uses deep but relatively narrow architectures. Table 2 does not specify whether reported accuracy is training or test accuracy. Exact results for the interblock-LIF removal auxiliary experiment are only shown in Figure 2; no uncertainty estimates are reported.

untested.parts: Near-zero training classification error in sufficiently large conventional CNNs, including random or corrupted labels and model-size or recipe qualifications.
Spurious minima and extra student neurons in two-layer ReLU teacher-student problems.
Training-error degradation and its prevention by identity shortcuts in conventional batch-normalized CNNs; longer-training controls; special initialization and normalization-free exceptions.
Activation-matched initialization, signal and gradient propagation, orthogonal versus Gaussian weights, and initialization-dependent trainable depth.
Learning-rate stability thresholds, loss recovery, curvature changes, edge-of-stability dynamics, and divergence.
Controlled effects of batch normalization on training speed and learning-rate tolerance, and Fixup comparisons.

record.verdict_notes: Remove the record's V3 verdicts. Different SNN block designs do not challenge or qualify V3's stated ANN results. The supplied text explicitly mentions training degradation, but Table 2 does not identify its accuracy split. N.A. entries cannot be interpreted as divergence or failed optimization.

versions.untested_parts: Zero or near-zero training classification error, random or corrupted labels, and the stated model-size and recipe conditions.
Two-layer ReLU teacher-student problems, spurious minima, and student width relative to teacher width.
ImageNet and CIFAR-10 claims about batch-normalized ANN convolutional networks and identity shortcuts specifically; the paper tests CIFAR-10 SNNs and modified spiking residual blocks.
Initialization comparisons, signal or gradient propagation, and trainable depth as a function of initialization.
Learning rates above stability thresholds, curvature or sharpness, recovery, and divergence.
Batch normalization's effect on training speed or learning-rate tolerance and Fixup without normalization.

relation.reason: Residual learning supplies the architectural approach; the experiments do not test any claim version on the systems and measures those versions specify.

tranche.reason: The study uses residual learning to develop and evaluate spiking-network architectures. Its SNN degradation results concern a different kind of system from V3's conventional ANNs.

source_check.notes: The introduction explicitly describes degradation in both training and testing accuracy for transplanted SNN ResNets, but Table 2 does not identify its accuracy split. The authors' conclusion about redesigned blocks enabling 482-layer CIFAR-10 and 104-layer ImageNet SNNs is accurately represented.
